211.title: Cut down the forest (280–289)
211.hook: cut down the whole forest of desire, not just one tree; death sweeps off the distracted like a flood a sleeping village
211.howItsDone: Teachers in many Buddhist traditions quote the forest verse when explaining that practice aims at craving itself, not only at its separate outlets; monks and lay students often memorize the Pali line.

segments.voice: Yesterday, all created things, and your line: all things pass. What three changing things did you watch? Day two hundred eleven, and the last day of chapter twenty, the way.

You decide to quit one thing. Say it's the late-night snack. You keep the promise for a week, and you feel strong. Then you notice you're scrolling until one in the morning instead. Or buying things you don't need. The snack was gone, but whatever wanted the snack just found another door. Anyone who has tried to change a habit knows this game of whack-a-mole. Today's verses name it with a picture that has made readers smile for two thousand years, because it's also a pun. Today: cut down the forest.
screen: `QUIT ONE THING.` → `IT COMES BACK SOMEWHERE ELSE.` → `A PICTURE, AND A PUN.`

segments.voice: Verses two hundred eighty to two hundred eighty-nine close the chapter on the way. They open with a warning about the young and strong who never get around to rousing themselves: the path doesn't walk itself. Then verse two hundred eighty-three, in Max Müller's English: "Cut down the whole forest of desire, not a tree only!" Here's the pun. In Pali, the word vana means a forest, and vana also means desire, longing. So the Buddha is saying: cut down the vana, the forest and the wanting both. Not one tree. You can chop down the snack tree, and the forest simply grows another one next to it. The verse goes on: when you've cleared both the forest and the undergrowth, you are free of the woods. The next verses show how deep the roots go. As long as desire is not cut, the mind stays tied, the text says, like a calf that won't leave its mother's side. Then comes the sharpest picture in the chapter. A man, proud of his children and his herds, with his mind on everything else, is carried off by death the way a flood carries off a sleeping village. In the night, while everyone dreams. The verses aren't trying to frighten. They're saying that time is the one thing desire keeps us from noticing. Sons and fathers and relatives can't shelter anyone from it, the text goes on, and so the wise person, seeing this, clears the road now. Buddhist teachers read this as practical advice. Cutting one tree is still worth doing. But the aim is to look past the tree to the forest, the wanting underneath, and to start while the village is still awake.
screen: `ROUSE YOURSELF: THE PATH WON'T WALK ITSELF.` · `VANA — FOREST, AND DESIRE.` · `THE FLOOD AND THE SLEEPING VILLAGE.` · `CLEAR THE ROAD NOW.` · then, large: `CUT THE FOREST.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and let the breath settle. Think of one small desire that came up today. A snack, a purchase, a check of the phone. Just one tree. Now, gently, look behind it. What was the wanting underneath? Boredom, maybe, or tiredness, or wanting to feel a little better. Don't fight it. Just see the forest behind the tree, and name it quietly to yourself. Then let the naming go and come back to the breath, in and out. The bell holds the time.
Cut down the forest. In Pali, vana is both a forest and a desire: cut the whole wanting, not one tree.
Your line: cut the forest. Today, trim one desire, just one, and when it tries to pop up somewhere else, smile at the forest. Day two hundred eleven.

fork.setup: you quit one habit, and the same restlessness shows up in a new one. what does verse 283 point you toward?
options: cut that one new tree even harder.

fork.reveal: the verse says cut the whole forest of desire, not a tree only: the outlets matter less than the wanting that feeds them.

original.note: Pali vana: a forest, and also desire; verse 283 plays on both.

trapdoor: what you thought: 'cut down the forest' is about chopping trees.
what it means: cut down desire itself, not just one of its outlets.
what a scholar hears: the Pali 'vanam chindatha ma rukkham' turns on vana (forest) and vana (desire); Müller flagged the pun in a note.

212.title: The bigger joy (290–295)
212.hook: if by leaving a small pleasure one finds a great one, the wise leave the small
212.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers often use verse 290 to explain renunciation not as loss but as trading a lesser happiness for a greater one; the riddle verses 294–295 are usually taught with the commentary's symbolic reading.

segments.voice: Yesterday, cut down the forest, and your line: cut the forest. Did the desire you trimmed pop up somewhere else? Day two hundred twelve, and chapter twenty-one begins.
screen: `CUT DOWN THE FOREST — CUT THE FOREST.`

segments.voice: There's a famous experiment with children and marshmallows. One now, or two if you can wait. Most of us know how that feels from the inside: the phone at dinner, when you'd really rather talk to the person across the table. The extra hour in bed, when you'd rather have the quiet morning walk. It isn't that the small pleasure is evil. It's that it sits right in front of the bigger one, blocking the view. A chapter the translator simply called miscellaneous opens with exactly this trade. Today: the bigger joy.
screen: `ONE MARSHMALLOW NOW, OR TWO?` → `THE SMALL PLEASURE BLOCKS THE VIEW.` → `A CHAPTER CALLED MISCELLANEOUS.`

segments.voice: Chapter twenty-one is a gathering of verses that didn't fit elsewhere, and it starts with one of the clearest in the book. Verse two hundred ninety, in Max Müller's English: "If by leaving a small pleasure one sees a great pleasure, let a wise man leave the small pleasure, and look to the great." Notice the verse doesn't say pleasure is bad. The Pali word is sukha, which means happiness, ease, sweetness. The verse wants more of it, not less. It's a trade, and the wise person makes the good one. The next verse tells you what a bad trade looks like: the one who seeks happiness for himself by causing pain to others gets tangled up in hatred and never gets free. Then the verses turn to attention. People neglect what ought to be done and do what ought not, the text says, and their troubles grow; but those who keep watch over the body, moment by moment, don't drift that way. Then comes the strangest pair of verses in the whole book, two hundred ninety-four and two hundred ninety-five. They say the true brahmana goes free, even after killing mother and father and two kings. Read on its own, it's shocking. The old commentary explains it as a riddle. The mother is craving, the father is pride, the kings are two wrong views, and the kingdom is the senses and everything that rides on them. Kill those, and you walk free. It's the forest from yesterday, told as a riddle. The bigger joy, in the end, is the freedom on the far side of all the small trades.
screen: `SUKHA — HAPPINESS, EASE, SWEETNESS.` · `A BAD TRADE: JOY BUILT ON PAIN.` · `KEEP WATCH OVER THE BODY.` · `THE RIDDLE OF MOTHER, FATHER, KINGS.` · then, large: `THE BIGGER JOY.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably. Bring to mind one small pleasure you reach for most days. Nothing dramatic: a snack, a scroll, a few more minutes in bed. Now ask, quietly, what bigger joy it sometimes stands in front of. A conversation, a rested morning, a clear head. You don't have to give anything up yet. Just see the two side by side, the small and the great. Then let both go, and rest in the breath, which asks nothing of you. The bell holds the time.
The bigger joy. Leave a small pleasure when it hides a great one: the verse wants more happiness, not less.
Your line: the bigger joy. Today, trade one small pleasure for the bigger one it was hiding, and notice how the trade feels afterward. Day two hundred twelve.
